testing_capacity.notes: The institute's evaluation note of 2 October 2026 reports its own cyber capability evaluation of Claude Opus 4.8, carried out in June 2026. An older Cabinet Office draft of 7 April 2026 said: '主要国AISIのように、技術評価のR＆Dリソース・体制が十分になく、自らAI評価ツールを作ったり、評価することができていない。' (unlike major countries' institutes, it lacks sufficient R&D resources and structures for technical evaluation, and has not been able to build AI evaluation tools or carry out evaluations itself) and '現在は、パートナー協定を結んでいる国研（NICT、産総研、NII、理研、IPA等）の成果を活用するのみ。最近、民間企業への外注を開始。' (at present it only uses the outputs of the national research institutes with which it has partnership agreements, such as NICT, AIST, NII, RIKEN and IPA, and it recently began outsourcing to private companies); the newer statement decides. The Cabinet-decided AI Basic Plan of July 2026 sets out a stronger evaluation role. Joint network testing reported, 2025-06-26 (multilingual exercise: 'Australia and Japan also ran independent tests in Mandarin Chinese and Japanese') and 2025-07-17 (agentic exercise).

model_access.notes: The June 2026 evaluation of Claude Opus 4.8 ran with the real-time cyber safeguards normally applied in deployment removed; the note does not say how that access was provided. No legal power, and no agreement providing for access to or evaluation of a frontier developer's models, was found. Agreements with such developers provide for neither access to nor evaluation of their models: the Anthropic memorandum of cooperation (29 October 2025) is 'an agreement to conduct the exchange of information and best practices on methods for companies to evaluate capabilities, limitations, and risks of AI models', and the OpenAI memorandum (29 May 2026) only explores cooperation on safety evaluation and benchmarks. Anthropic's announcement of 31 March 2026 refers to 'the arrangements we have with safety institutes in the US, UK, and Japan, where early access and technical information sharing has helped governments', which is undated and names no model. The AI Promotion Act (Act No. 53 of 2025) does not mention the institute. The report of 30 October 2026 says GLM-5.3, GLM-5.2 and Claude Opus 4.8 were used via API; it describes no access beyond that, so it is not counted as an access event.

claims.text: Kenji Hiramoto took office as the institute's full-time secretary-general on 14 February 2024.
The AI Basic Plan says the institute needs further strengthening and lists active evaluation of high-performance AI to deter events that threaten national security among the work to advance.
Evaluated the cyber capabilities of Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8.
Released an AI safety evaluation tool as open-source software.
Commissioned the 'Report on the Specific Influence on AI Safety', with NRI SecureTechnologies as research contractor.
Published a guide to evaluation perspectives that AI system developers and providers can refer to when conducting AI safety evaluations.
Published the second edition of its overview of known attacks on AI systems and their impacts.
Is tasked with international cooperation with bodies in other countries, such as the UK and US AI Safety Institutes.
Its team took part in the network's second joint testing exercise, on multilingual testing.
Led the launch of a discussion framework aimed at building AI safety benchmarks and held its kick-off in October 2025.
Took part in government discussions on the procurement and use of AI, led by the Digital Agency and other bodies, and made proposals for addressing the risks of generative AI.
It says its tasks include research on safety standards, checking tools, disinformation countermeasure technology, and AI and cybersecurity.
Has given lectures and conducted training, 14 times in total.
